title: Strategy pattern
idea: The Strategy pattern puts each interchangeable algorithm behind one interface, so a context class calls it without knowing which version runs.

analogy.text: A map app asks how you travel: car, bike or on foot. The same trip gets a different route, and the app's screen never changes.
analogy.breaks: You pick the mode; in code, configuration or a factory usually picks.

points: A context holds a strategy interface and delegates one decision to it.
Adding an algorithm means adding a class, not editing a growing `if` chain.
The JDK uses it: `List.sort` takes a `Comparator` that decides the order.
Skip it for two stable branches; a plain `if` reads better there.

hero.title: Checkout delegates pricing to a strategy

steps.caption: Configuration builds the strategies and hands them to `Checkout` through its constructor.
`Checkout` validates the weight, then looks up the rate for the chosen method.
It calls `centsFor` on the interface. It never asks which class it got.
`WeightRate` serves standard and express. Same class, different numbers.
A lambda fits too, because `ShippingRate` has exactly one abstract method.
A new delivery method is one new class. `Checkout` stays untouched: the Open/Closed Principle (OCP).

code.title: The problem: if chain
code.caption: Every pricing rule lives in one method, and the last `else` swallows typos.

walk.text: One method owns every pricing rule, so each new delivery method edits this class.
Rules hide in branches. You cannot test express pricing apart from the rest.
A drone rule with a weight limit makes the chain harder to read again.
The final `else` catches every unknown string and charges it as standard.
The output proves it: "Express" gets a wrong price instead of a loud failure.

code.title: The fix: strategies
code.caption: One interface, swappable implementations, and a context that only delegates.

walk.text: The strategy interface has one method, so lambdas can implement it.
A record strategy. Its compact constructor rejects negative rates up front.
`Map.copyOf` makes the context immutable; later changes to the caller's map cannot leak in.
Validate, look up the strategy, and fail loudly on an unknown key.
Strategies are chosen at the edge. A `TreeMap` keeps the printed order stable.
The typo that was mispriced before is now rejected with a clear message.

pitfalls: A context that checks `instanceof` on its strategy has rebuilt the `if` chain; keep it blind.
Strategies with shared mutable fields break when threads share them; keep them stateless or immutable.
Creating strategies with `new` inside the context hard-codes them again; inject them from outside.

quiz.why: `reversed()` puts longer names first. `List.sort` is stable, so the tied names keep their original relative order.

takeaway: Strategy swaps how a step is done; the calling code never changes.
